plain_english: This thought can also help keep you from being proud of yourself. Remember that you can never earn the praise given to someone who has lived as a philosopher his whole life, or at least since he was young. Everyone knows — especially you — that you have done many things that go against that perfect way of living. You have gotten off track. It will be hard now to earn back the name and respect of a philosopher. Your actual job and duties work against this too. So if you truly understand what really matters, don't worry about your reputation. Let it be enough that you spend the rest of your life — however long or short — living as your nature requires, according to your true purpose. Work to understand what your nature needs. Don't let anything else pull you away from that.
original_excerpt: This also, among other things, may serve to keep thee from vainglory; if thou shalt consider, that thou art now altogether incapable of the commendation of one, who all his life long, or from his youth at least, hath lived a philosopher's life. For both unto others, and to thyself especially, it is well known, that thou hast done many things contrary to that perfection of life. Thou hast therefore been confounded in thy course, and henceforth it will be hard for thee to recover the title and credit of a philosopher. And to it also is thy calling and profession repugnant. If therefore thou dost truly understand, what it is that is of moment indeed; as for thy fame and credit, take no thought or care for that: let it suffice thee if all the rest of thy life, be it more or less, thou shalt live as thy nature requireth, or according to the true and natural end of thy making. Take pains therefore to know what it is that thy nature requireth, and let nothing else distract thee.

plain_english: You have enough experience now. You have searched in many places and made many mistakes. You could not find happiness in any of them. Not in clever arguments and logic. Not in wealth. Not in honor and reputation. Not in pleasure. None of these worked. So where can happiness be found? In doing what human nature requires. How do you do that? By having the right beliefs and opinions. These guide all your actions. What are the right beliefs? These: nothing is truly good for a person except what makes them just, self-controlled, brave, and generous. And nothing is truly bad except what prevents these qualities.
original_excerpt: Thou hast already had sufficient experience, that of those many things that hitherto thou hast erred and wandered about, thou couldst not find happiness in any of them. Not in syllogisms, and logical subtilties, not in wealth, not in honour and reputation, not in pleasure. In none of all these. Wherein then is it to be found? In the practice of those things, which the nature of man, as he is a man, doth require. How then shall he do those things? if his dogmata, or moral tenets and opinions (from which all motions and actions do proceed), be right and true. Which be those dogmata? Those that concern that which is good or evil, as that there is nothing truly good and beneficial unto man, but that which makes him just, temperate, courageous, liberal; and that there is nothing truly evil and hurtful unto man, but that which causeth the contrary effects.

plain_english: Before every action you're about to take, ask yourself this question: How will this sit with me once it's done? Will I regret it? In just a little while I'll be dead and gone, and everything will be over. What more do I need to care about than this: that whatever I'm doing right now is the right action for a reasonable person? Someone whose goal is the common good. Someone who follows the same law of justice and reason that God himself follows.
original_excerpt: Upon every action that thou art about, put this question to thyself; How will this when it is done agree with me? Shall I have no occasion to repent of it? Yet a very little while and I am dead and gone; and all things are at end. What then do I care for more than this, that my present action whatsoever it be, may be the proper action of one that is reasonable; whose end is, the common good; who in all things is ruled and governed by the same law of right and reason, by which God Himself is.

plain_english: Alexander, Caesar, Pompey — what are they compared to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? These philosophers saw into the true nature of things. They understood causes and subjects deeply. That's where they had real power and authority. But those conquerors? Their slavery went as far as their errors did.
original_excerpt: Alexander, Caius, Pompeius; what are these to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? These penetrated into the true nature of things; into all causes, and all subjects: and upon these did they exercise their power and authority. But as for those, as the extent of their error was, so far did their slavery extend.

plain_english: What they have done, they will keep doing, even if you killed yourself over it. First, don't let it bother you. All things, good and bad, happen according to the nature of the universe. And very soon, everything will be over. No one will be remembered — just look at Africanus and Augustus. It's already happening to them. Second, focus on the thing itself. Look at it clearly. Remember that you are still bound to be a good person. Remember what your nature demands of you as a human being. Don't be pulled away from what you're doing. Say what seems most just to you. But say it kindly, humbly, and honestly.
original_excerpt: What they have done, they will still do, although thou shouldst hang thyself. First; let it not trouble thee. For all things both good and evil: come to pass according to the nature and general condition of the universe, and within a very little while, all things will be at an end; no man will be remembered: as now of Africanus (for example) and Augustus it is already come to pass. Then secondly; fix thy mind upon the thing itself; look into it, and remembering thyself, that thou art bound nevertheless to be a good man, and what it is that thy nature requireth of thee as thou art a man, be not diverted from what thou art about, and speak that which seemeth unto thee most just: only speak it kindly, modestly, and without hypocrisy.

plain_english: The universe is always busy doing one thing: moving what is here to somewhere else, changing it, then taking it away and carrying it to another place. So you don't need to fear anything new. Everything follows the same patterns. Everything is distributed fairly.
original_excerpt: That which the nature of the universe doth busy herself about, is; that which is here, to transfer it thither, to change it, and thence again to take it away, and to carry it to another place. So that thou needest not fear any new thing. For all things are usual and ordinary; and all things are disposed by equality.

plain_english: Every nature finds contentment when it follows its proper path. A rational nature succeeds when it does three things. First, it doesn't accept ideas that are false or uncertain. Second, in all its actions and decisions, it aims only at the common good. It wants nothing and avoids nothing except what is within its own power to achieve or prevent. And finally, it willingly and gladly accepts whatever the universal nature assigns to it.
original_excerpt: Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course it speeds. A reasonable nature doth then speed, when first in matter of fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either false uncertain. Secondly, when in all its motions and resolutions it takes its level at the common good only, and that it desireth nothing, and flieth from nothing, bet what is in its own power to compass or avoid. And lastly, when it willingly and gladly embraceth, whatsoever is dealt and appointed unto it by the common nature.

plain_english: A leaf is part of the nature of all plants and trees. But a leaf's nature is part of something without reason or feeling — something that can be blocked from its purpose and is enslaved to outside forces. Human nature is different. It's part of a common nature that can't be hindered, and which is both reasonable and just. This is why nature distributes all things fairly — time, substance, form, action, and events. But don't expect to find perfect equality in each thing by itself. Instead, look at all the parts of one thing together, and compare that whole with all the parts of another thing together.
original_excerpt: For it is part of it; even as the nature of any one leaf, is part of the common nature of all plants and trees. But that the nature of a leaf, is part of a nature both unreasonable and unsensible, and which in its proper end may be hindered; or, which is servile and slavish: whereas the nature of man is part of a common nature which cannot be hindered, and which is both reasonable and just. From whence also it is, that according to the worth of everything, she doth make such equal distribution of all things, as of duration, substance form, operation, and of events and accidents. But herein consider not whether thou shalt find this equality in everything absolutely and by itself; but whether in all the particulars of some one thing taken together, and compared with all the particulars of some other thing, and them together likewise.

plain_english: You don't have time to read. So what? Don't you have time to train yourself? To not harm yourself? To fight against physical pleasures and pains and overcome them? To look down on honor and fame? And not just to avoid getting angry at people who are ungrateful and indifferent toward you — but to still care for them and their well-being?
original_excerpt: Thou hast no time nor opportunity to read. What then? Hast thou not time and opportunity to exercise thyself, not to wrong thyself; to strive against all carnal pleasures and pains, and to get the upper hand of them; to contemn honour and vainglory; and not only, not to be angry with them, whom towards thee thou doest find unsensible and unthankful; but also to have a care of them still, and of their welfare?

plain_english: Stop complaining about the troubles of court life. Don't do it in public with others, and don't do it in private to yourself.
original_excerpt: Forbear henceforth to complain of the trouble of a courtly life, either in public before others, or in private by thyself.

plain_english: Regret is blaming yourself for missing or skipping something that would have helped you. Whatever is good is also helpful. An honest, good person values these things and treats them seriously. But no honest, good person ever regrets missing out on bodily pleasures. So bodily pleasures are neither good nor helpful.
original_excerpt: Repentance is an inward and self-reprehension for the neglect or omission of somewhat that was profitable. Now whatsoever is good, is also profitable, and it is the part of an honest virtuous man to set by it, and to make reckoning of it accordingly. But never did any honest virtuous man repent of the neglect or omission of any carnal pleasure: no carnal pleasure then is either good or profitable.

plain_english: When something comes up, ask yourself: What is this thing really? What is it made of? What is it supposed to do? What caused it? Why does it exist in this world, and how long will it last? This is how you must examine everything that comes your way.
original_excerpt: This, what is it in itself, and by itself, according to its proper constitution? What is the substance of it? What is the matter, or proper use? What is the form or efficient cause? What is it for in this world, and how long will it abide? Thus must thou examine all things, that present themselves unto thee.

plain_english: When you find it hard to get out of bed in the morning, remind yourself of this: doing things that help others is what your nature requires. It's what being human means. But sleeping? Even animals do that. What could be more natural and satisfying than living according to your true nature?
original_excerpt: When thou art hard to be stirred up and awaked out of thy sleep, admonish thyself and call to mind, that, to perform actions tending to the common good is that which thine own proper constitution, and that which the nature of man do require. But to sleep, is common to unreasonable creatures also. And what more proper and natural, yea what more kind and pleasing, than that which is according to nature?

plain_english: When any thought or image comes into your mind, look at what it really is. See its true nature and qualities. Think it through carefully.
original_excerpt: As every fancy and imagination presents itself unto thee, consider (if it be possible) the true nature, and the proper qualities of it, and reason with thyself about it.

plain_english:
When you first meet someone, ask yourself right away: What does this person think is good or bad? What are their views on pain and pleasure? On honor and shame? On life and death? Once you understand their beliefs, their actions make perfect sense. If someone holds certain opinions, of course they will act accordingly. Remember that they cannot help but do what they do, given what they believe.

It would be foolish to be surprised that a fig tree grows figs. In the same way, it's foolish to be surprised that the world produces whatever it naturally produces. A doctor shouldn't be shocked when someone gets sick. A ship captain shouldn't be amazed when the wind changes direction.
original_excerpt: At thy first encounter with any one, say presently to thyself: This man, what are his opinions concerning that which is good or evil? as concerning pain, pleasure, and the causes of both; concerning honour, and dishonour, concerning life and death? thus and thus. Now if it be no wonder that a man should have such and such opinions, how can it be a wonder that he should do such and such things? I will remember then, that he cannot but do as he doth, holding those opinions that he doth. Remember, that as it is a shame for any man to wonder that a fig tree should bear figs, so also to wonder that the world should bear anything, whatsoever it is which in the ordinary course of nature it may bear. To a physician also and to a pilot it is a shame either for the one to wonder, that such and such a one should have an ague; or for the other, that the winds should prove Contrary.

plain_english: Remember, it's just as honest to change your mind when you need to and follow someone who can correct you as it is to figure out what's right on your own from the start. Nothing is asked of you that goes beyond your own thinking and judgment and understanding.
original_excerpt: Remember, that to change thy mind upon occasion, and to follow him that is able to rectify thee, is equally ingenuous, as to find out at the first, what is right and just, without help. For of thee nothing is required, ti, is beyond the extent of thine own deliberation and jun. merit, and of thine own understanding.

plain_english: If this were your doing and in your power, would you do it? If it's not your doing, who are you blaming? The atoms, or the gods? Either way, that's madness. So blame no one. If it's in your power, fix what's wrong. If it's not, what's the point of complaining? Nothing should be done without a purpose.
original_excerpt: If it were thine act and in thine own power, wouldest thou do it? If it were not, whom dost tin accuse? the atoms, or the Gods? For to do either, the part of a mad man. Thou must therefore blame nobody, but if it be in thy power, redress what is amiss; if it be not, to what end is it to complain? For nothing should be done but to some certain end.

plain_english: Whatever dies and falls, no matter how or where it happens, it cannot fall outside the world. Here it lives and changes, and here it breaks down into its basic parts. These are the same elements that make up the world and make up you. When they change, they don't complain. Why should you?
original_excerpt: Whatsoever dieth and falleth, however and wheresoever it die and fall, it cannot fall out of the world, here it have its abode and change, here also shall it have its dissolution into its proper elements. The same are the world's elements, and the elements of which thou dost consist. And they when they are changed, they murmur not; why shouldest thou?

plain_english: Everything was made for a purpose. A horse has a purpose. A vine has a purpose. Why are you surprised by this? Even the sun would say, "I was made for something." Every god has its own job to do. So what were you made for? To play around and have fun? See how even basic common sense can't accept that.
original_excerpt: Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine. Why wonderest thou? The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for something; and so hath every god its proper function. What then were then made for? to disport and delight thyself? See how even common sense and reason cannot brook it.

plain_english: Nature has its purpose in how things end, just as much as in how they begin and continue.
original_excerpt: Nature hath its end as well in the end and final consummation of anything that is, as in the begin-nine and continuation of it.

plain_english: Think of someone tossing up a ball. Is the ball better when it goes up? Is it worse when it comes down or hits the ground? What about a bubble — is it better if it lasts longer? Is it worse if it pops? The same with a candle. This is how you should think about fame and death.
original_excerpt: As one that tosseth up a ball. And what is a ball the better, if the motion of it be upwards; or the worse if it be downwards; or if it chance to fall upon the ground? So for the bubble; if it continue, what it the better? and if it dissolve, what is it the worse And so is it of a candle too. And so must thou reason with thyself, both in matter of fame, and in matter of death.

plain_english: As for the body itself — the thing that dies — do you want to know how base it really is? Look at it from every angle, not just when it appears pleasant. How does it look when it's old and wrinkled? When it's sick and in pain? When it's caught up in lust and sexual desire?
original_excerpt: For as for the body itself, (the subject of death) wouldest thou know the vileness of it? Turn it about that thou mayest behold it the worst sides upwards as well, as in its more ordinary pleasant shape; how doth it look, when it is old and withered? when sick and pained? when in the act of lust, and fornication?

plain_english: And as for fame. This life is short. The one who praises and the one who is praised will both soon be dust. The one who remembers and the one who is remembered will both soon be dust. Besides, you are only praised in one small corner of the world. And even in that corner, not everyone praises you. No one does it constantly. And yet the whole earth itself is just one tiny point compared to the entire universe.
original_excerpt: And as for fame. This life is short. Both he that praiseth, and he that is praised; he that remembers, and he that is remembered, will soon be dust and ashes. Besides, it is but in one corner of this part of the world that thou art praised; and yet in this corner, thou hast not the joint praises of all men; no nor scarce of any one constantly. And yet the whole earth itself, what is it but as one point, in regard of the whole world?

plain_english: Whatever you're thinking about falls into one of these categories: the thing itself, the belief about it, how it works, or what it really means.
original_excerpt: That which must be the subject of thy consideration, is either the matter itself, or the dogma, or the operation, or the true sense and signification.

plain_english: These things happened to you for good reason. So why don't you change? But you would rather become good tomorrow than today.
original_excerpt: Most justly have these things happened unto thee: why dost not thou amend? O but thou hadst rather become good to-morrow, than to be so to-day.

plain_english: Should I do this? Yes, I will — as long as my action helps people. Does something difficult or painful happen to me? I accept it, knowing it comes from the gods and their care for all things. Everything that happens flows from that same source.
original_excerpt: Shall I do it? I will; so the end of my action be to do good unto men. Doth anything by way of cross or adversity happen unto me? I accept it, with reference unto the Gods, and their providence; the fountain of all things, from which whatsoever comes to pass, doth hang and depend.

plain_english: Judge everything else by one example: this bathing that takes up so much of our time — what is it really? Oil, sweat, dirt. The grime of the body. A sticky mess of oils and lotions mixed with bodily filth. All of it base and disgusting. And this is what almost every part of our life is like. Every worldly thing.
original_excerpt: By one action judge of the rest: this bathing which usually takes up so much of our time, what is it? Oil, sweat, filth; or the sordes of the body: an excrementitious viscosity, the excrements of oil and other ointments used about the body, and mixed with the sordes of the body: all base and loathsome. And such almost is every part of our life; and every worldly object.

plain_english: Lucilla buried Verus; then others buried Lucilla herself. So Secunda buried Maximus, then Secunda herself was buried. So Epitynchanus buried Diotimus; then Epitynchanus himself was buried. So Antoninus Pius buried his wife Faustina; then Antoninus himself was buried. This is how the world works. First Celer buried Adrianus; then Adrianus himself was buried. And those serious, stern men — those who predicted other people's deaths, those who were so proud and grand — where are they now? I mean those stern ones like Charax, Demetrius the Platonic, and Eudaemon, and others like them. They lasted only a day. All dead and gone long ago. Some were forgotten the moment they died. Others became stories. And even those stories are now forgotten too.
original_excerpt: Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others. So Secunda Maximus, then Secunda herself. So Epitynchanus, Diotimus; then Epitynchanus himself. So Antoninus Pius, Faustina his wife; then Antoninus himself. This is the course of the world. First Celer, Adrianus; then Adrianus himself. And those austere ones; those that foretold other men's deaths; those that were so proud and stately, where are they now? Those austere ones I mean, such as were Charax, and Demetrius the Platonic, and Eudaemon, and others like unto those. They were all but for one day; all dead and gone long since. Some of them no sooner dead, than forgotten. Others soon turned into fables. Of others, even that which was fabulous, is now long since forgotten.

plain_english: Remember this: whatever you are made of will soon scatter apart. Your life and breath, or your soul, will either be no more or will be moved to some other place.
original_excerpt: This thereafter thou must remember, that whatsoever thou art compounded of, shall soon be dispersed, and that thy life and breath, or thy soul, shall either be no more or shall ranslated (sp.), and appointed to some certain place and station.

plain_english: The real joy of a person is to do what humans are meant to do. What humans are meant to do is this: first, to be kind to other people. Second, to control physical desires and urges. Third, to see through appealing but false ideas. Fourth, to think about the nature of the universe and what happens in it.
original_excerpt: The true joy of a man, is to do that which properly belongs unto a man. That which is most proper unto a man, is, first, to be kindly affected towards them that are of the same kind and nature as he is himself to contemn all sensual motions and appetites, to discern rightly all plausible fancies and imaginations, to contemplate the nature of the universe; both it, and things that are done in it.

plain_english: When you think about what happens to you, consider three things. First, look at the immediate cause — what seems to have caused it. Second, look at the ultimate source — God, from whom everything in the world comes. Third, think about the people around you — how can this be useful to them?
original_excerpt: In which kind of contemplation three several relations are to be observed The first, to the apparent secondary cause. The Second to the first original cause, God, from whom originally proceeds whatsoever doth happen in the world. The third and last, to them that we live and converse with: what use may be made of it, to their use and benefit.

plain_english: If pain is an evil, it must affect either the body or the soul. It can't be the body, because the body itself feels nothing. So it must be the soul. But the soul has the power to keep its own peace and not think that pain is evil. All judgment and choice comes from within. The sense of evil cannot get in there unless we let it in through our own opinions.
original_excerpt: If pain be an evil, either it is in regard of the body; (and that cannot be, because the body of itself is altogether insensible:) or in regard of the soul But it is in the power of the soul, to preserve her own peace and tranquillity, and not to suppose that pain is evil. For all judgment and deliberation; all prosecution, or aversation is from within, whither the sense of evil (except it be let in by opinion) cannot penetrate.

plain_english: Push away all pointless thoughts. Keep telling yourself: Right now, if I choose, I can keep my soul free of all evil, all desire, all worry and confusion. Instead, I can see things as they really are and treat everything according to its true value. Remember this power that nature has given you.
original_excerpt: Wipe off all idle fancies, and say unto thyself incessantly; Now if I will, it is in my power to keep out of this my soul all wickedness, all lust, and concupiscences, all trouble and confusion. But on the contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true worth. Remember then this thy power that nature hath given thee.

plain_english: Whether you speak in the Senate or to any person, let your words always be serious and humble. But don't make a show of using perfect formal language about what is truly good and truly noble. Don't parade your knowledge about the emptiness of the world and worldly people, even though truth and reason tell you these things.
original_excerpt: Whether thou speak in the Senate or whether thou speak to any particular, let thy speech In always grave and modest. But thou must not openly and vulgarly observe that sound and exact form of speaking, concerning that which is truly good and truly civil; the vanity of the world, and of worldly men: which otherwise truth and reason doth prescribe.

plain_english: Augustus and his whole court: his wife, his daughter, his nephews, his sons-in-law, his sister, Agrippa, his relatives, his servants, his friends, Areus, Maecenas, his priests who killed animals for sacrifice and fortune-telling. There you have the death of an entire court. Now think of all the others who have died since Augustus. Did death treat them any differently — even though they were so many and so grand while they lived — than it treats any ordinary person?
original_excerpt: Augustus his court; his wife, his daughter, his nephews, his sons-in-law his sister, Agrippa, his kinsmen, his domestics, his friends; Areus, Mæcenas, his slayers of beasts for sacrifice and divination: there thou hast the death of a whole court together. Proceed now on to the rest that have been since that of Augustus. Hath death dwelt with them otherwise, though so many and so stately whilst they lived, than it doth use to deal with any one particular man?

plain_english: Think about the death of an entire family line, like what happened to the Pompeys. You see it written on tombstones: "He was the last of his family." Think of all the care his ancestors took to leave behind children. Yet in the end, someone must always be the last. So here again, consider how whole families die out completely.
original_excerpt: Consider now the death of a whole kindred and family, as of that of the Pompeys, as that also that useth to be written upon some monuments, HE WAS THE LAST OF HIS OWN KINDRED. O what care did his predecessors take, that they might leave a successor, yet behold at last one or other must of necessity be THE LAST. Here again therefore consider the death of a whole kindred.

plain_english: Focus your whole life on doing one thing at a time. If you do what is right in each action with all your power, that should be enough. Who can stop you from doing what is right? You might say there are outside obstacles. But nothing can stop you from acting justly, with self-control, and in a way that honors God. Yes, but something might block a specific task you planned. Then be content with that obstacle itself. Turn your mind gently toward what is actually possible instead of what you first intended. Let a new action take the place of the old one. This new action fits just as well with this focused way of living we're talking about.
original_excerpt: Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee. And who can hinder thee, but that thou mayest perform what is fitting? But there may be some outward let and impediment. Not any, that can hinder thee, but that whatsoever thou dost, thou may do it, justly, temperately, and with the praise of God. Yea, but there may be somewhat, whereby some operation or other of thine may be hindered. And then, with that very thing that doth hinder, thou mayest he well pleased, and so by this gentle and equanimious conversion of thy mind unto that which may be, instead of that which at first thou didst intend, in the room of that former action there succeedeth another, which agrees as well with this contraction of thy life, that we now speak of.

plain_english: Accept good fortune without showing off when it comes. Then you will be able to let it go easily when it is taken away.
original_excerpt: Receive temporal blessings without ostentation, when they are sent and thou shalt be able to part with them with all readiness and facility when they are taken from thee again.

plain_english:
If you ever saw a hand, foot, or head lying somewhere by itself, cut off from the rest of the body, that's what you make yourself when you fight against what happens to you. You divide yourself from the whole. The same thing happens when you break the natural law that connects us all, or when you act without kindness toward others. When you do this, you cut yourself off from the unity that nature intended. You were born as a part of something larger, but now you have separated yourself.

But here's something to celebrate: you can be reunited again. God hasn't given this gift to any other part of creation. Once other things are cut off, they can't come back together. But look at this incredible goodness! It values human beings so much. At first, you were made so you didn't have to separate yourself from the whole unless you chose to. And even after you've cut yourself off, it's arranged so that if you want to, you can return. You can grow back together and take your place as part of the whole again.
original_excerpt: If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by itself, in some place or other, as cut off from the rest of the body, such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth, that either is offended with anything that is happened, (whatsoever it be) and as it were divides himself from it: or that commits anything against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men: or, he that, commits any act of uncharitableness. Whosoever thou art, thou art such, thou art cast forth I know not whither out of the general unity, which is according to nature. Thou went born indeed a part, but now thou hast cut thyself off. However, herein is matter of joy and exultation, that thou mayst be united again. God hath not granted it unto any other part, that once separated and cut off, it might be reunited, and come together again. But, behold, that GOODNESS how great and immense it is! which hath so much esteemed MAN. As at first he was so made, that he needed not, except he would himself, have divided himself from the whole; so once divided and cut off, IT hath so provided and ordered it, that if he would himself, he might return, and grow together again, and be admitted into its former rank and place of a part, as he was before.

plain_english: Nature has given thinking creatures many abilities. One special gift is this: when something opposes nature and fights against her plans, she finds a way to use it anyway. She makes it serve her purposes, even when it doesn't want to. Through this unwilling cooperation, she makes it part of herself whether it likes it or not. We can do the same thing. Whatever obstacles and problems we face in life, we can use them as tools. They can help us reach whatever goal we set for ourselves as our natural purpose and happiness.
original_excerpt: As almost all her other faculties and properties the nature of the universe hath imparted unto every reasonable creature, so this in particular we have received from her, that as whatsoever doth oppose itself unto her, and doth withstand her in her purposes and intentions, she doth, though against its will and intention, bring it about to herself, to serve herself of it in the execution of her own destinated ends; and so by this though not intended co-operation of it with herself makes it part of herself whether it will or no. So may every reasonable creature, what crosses and impediments soever it meets with in the course of this mortal life, it may use them as fit and proper objects, to the furtherance of whatsoever it intended and absolutely proposed unto itself as its natural end and happiness.

plain_english: Don't let the general misery of human life trouble you. Don't let your mind wander and pile up all the troubles and disasters you might face. Instead, when something specific happens, ask yourself: What exactly makes this present situation so unbearable? You'll be embarrassed to say. Then remember that neither the future nor the past can hurt you — only what's happening now. And even that becomes much smaller if you look at it closely. Then ask your mind if it can't handle this one brief moment with patience.
original_excerpt: Let not the general representation unto thyself of the wretchedness of this our mortal life, trouble thee. Let not thy mind wander up and down, and heap together in her thoughts the many troubles and grievous calamities which thou art as subject unto as any other. But as everything in particular doth happen, put this question unto thyself, and say: What is it that in this present matter, seems unto thee so intolerable? For thou wilt be ashamed to confess it. Then upon this presently call to mind, that neither that which is future, nor that which is past can hurt thee; but that only which is present. (And that also is much lessened, if thou dost lightly circumscribe it:) and then check thy mind if for so little a while, (a mere instant), it cannot hold out with patience.

plain_english: What's the point? Are Panthea or Pergamus still standing by their masters' tombs today? Are Chabrias or Diotimus still at Hadrian's grave? What foolishness! Even if they were, would their dead masters know? And if they knew, would they care? And if they cared, would that make these servants live forever? Weren't they also meant to grow old and die? And once they're dead, what happens to all that devotion? In the end, what is any of this for? We're all just bags of blood and flesh that rot away.
original_excerpt: What? are either Panthea or Pergamus abiding to this day by their masters' tombs? or either Chabrias or Diotimus by that of Adrianus? O foolery! For what if they did, would their masters be sensible of It? or if sensible, would they be glad of it? or if glad, were these immortal? Was not it appointed unto them also (both men and women,) to become old in time, and then to die? And these once dead, what would become of these former? And when all is done, what is all this for, but for a mere bag of blood and corruption?

plain_english:
If you have sharp eyes, use them for good judgment and wise choices, he says.

Looking at how people are made, I don't see any virtue that works against justice. But I do see one that can resist pleasure and self-indulgence: self-control.
original_excerpt:
If thou beest quick-sighted, be so in matter of judgment, and best discretion, saith he.

In the whole constitution of man, I see not any virtue contrary to justice, whereby it may be resisted and opposed. But one whereby pleasure and voluptuousness may be resisted and opposed, I see: continence.

plain_english: If you can drop your judgments about what seems harmful or offensive, you yourself are as safe as can be. You yourself? And who is that? Your reason. 'Yes, but I am not reason alone.' Fine. Even so, don't let your reason accept grief. And if there is anything in you that grieves, let that part — whatever it is — handle its own grief, if it can.
original_excerpt: If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.

plain_english:
Whatever blocks the senses is harmful to our sensing nature. Whatever blocks our desires and drives is harmful to that part of us. Just as with our sensing nature, whatever blocks our basic life functions is harmful to that part. And whatever blocks the mind and understanding must be harmful to our reasoning nature. Now think about yourself. Are you hit by pain or pleasure? Let your senses deal with that. Have you run into some obstacle in your plans? If you set your goal without thinking it through, then yes, your reasoning has taken a hit. But if you planned for whatever might happen, you are not hurt or truly blocked. In the things that belong to the mind, no one can stop you. Fire cannot reach it. Iron cannot reach it. No tyrant can reach it. No insulting words can reach it. Nothing else can get inside.

Once the mind is whole and complete, there is no fear it will ever change.
original_excerpt:
That which is a hindrance of the senses, is an evil to the sensitive nature. That which is a hindrance of the appetitive and prosecutive faculty, is an evil to the sensitive nature. As of the sensitive, so of the vegetative constitution, whatsoever is a hindrance unto it, is also in that respect an evil unto the same. And so likewise, whatsoever is a hindrance unto the mind and understanding, must needs be the proper evil of the reasonable nature. Now apply all those things unto thyself. Do either pain or pleasure seize on thee? Let the senses look to that. Hast thou met with Some obstacle or other in thy purpose and intention? If thou didst propose without due reservation and exception now hath thy reasonable part received a blow indeed But if in general thou didst propose unto thyself what soever might be, thou art not thereby either hurt, nor properly hindered. For in those things that properly belong unto the mind, she cannot be hindered by any man. It is not fire, nor iron; nor the power of a tyrant nor the power of a slandering tongue; nor anything else that can penetrate into her.

If once round and solid, there is no fear that ever it will change.

plain_english: Why should I trouble myself? I never willingly troubled anyone else. Different things bring joy to different people. This is what brings me joy: if my mind is clear and healthy, not turning away from any person, not rejecting the things that come with being human. If I can look at everything in the world with gentleness and kindness. If I can accept all things and treat everything according to its true worth.
original_excerpt: Why should I grieve myself; who never did willingly grieve any other! One thing rejoices one and another thing another. As for me, this is my joy, if my understanding be right and sound, as neither averse from any man, nor refusing any of those things which as a man I am subject unto; if I can look upon all things in the world meekly and kindly; accept all things and carry myself towards everything according to to true worth of the thing itself.

plain_english: Give this present moment to yourself. Those who chase fame after death don't realize something. The people who will remember them later will be just like the people they can barely stand now. And those future people will also die. But think about it clearly. What does it matter to you if many people make noise about you or have opinions about you?
original_excerpt: This time that is now present, bestow thou upon thyself. They that rather hunt for fame after death, do not consider, that those men that shall be hereafter, will be even such, as these whom now they can so hardly bear with. And besides they also will be mortal men. But to consider the thing in itself, if so many with so many voices, shall make such and such a sound, or shall have such and such an opinion concerning thee, what is it to thee?

plain_english: Take me and throw me wherever you want: it makes no difference to me. Wherever I land, I'll still have my inner spirit on my side. That spirit stays content with my steady character and with the actions that fit who I really am.
original_excerpt: Take me and throw me where thou wilt: I am indifferent. For there also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are suitable and agreeable.

plain_english: Is this really worth it? Is this worth letting my soul suffer and become worse than it was? Worth getting depressed, or worked up, or confused, or scared? What could possibly be so important that you should value it this much?
original_excerpt: Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified? What can there be, that thou shouldest so much esteem?

plain_english: Nothing can happen to you that isn't natural for a human being. Just as nothing happens to an ox, a vine, or a stone that isn't natural for those things. Everything gets what belongs to its own nature. So if nothing can happen that isn't both normal and natural, why are you upset? The nature that governs everything wouldn't bring something unbearable upon anyone.
original_excerpt: Nothing can happen unto thee, which is not incidental unto thee, as thou art a man. As nothing can happen either to an ox, a vine, or to a stone, which is not incidental unto them; unto every one in his own kind. If therefore nothing can happen unto anything, which is not both usual and natural; why art thou displeased? Sure the common nature of all would not bring anything upon any, that were intolerable.

plain_english: If something outside yourself causes your grief, know that it's not really the thing itself that hurts you. It's your own thoughts and judgments about it. You can change those thoughts whenever you want to. But if what grieves you is some flaw in your own character, then fix your beliefs and attitudes. If you're upset because you're not doing what seems right and just to you, why not just do it instead of being upset? Maybe something stronger than you is getting in the way. Then don't let it bother you, since it's not your fault the thing can't be done. 'But this is so important that life isn't worth living if I can't do it.' If that's true, then as long as you keep a kind and loving attitude toward everyone, you can go ahead and die. Even then, you're doing your best work when you die in peace with the very people who blocked you.
original_excerpt: If therefore it be a thing external that causes thy grief, know, that it is not that properly that doth cause it, but thine own conceit and opinion concerning the thing: which thou mayest rid thyself of, when thou wilt. But if it be somewhat that is amiss in thine own disposition, that doth grieve thee, mayest thou not rectify thy moral tenets and opinions. But if it grieve thee, that thou doest not perform that which seemeth unto thee right and just, why doest not thou choose rather to perform it than to grieve? But somewhat that is stronger than thyself doth hinder thee. Let it not grieve thee then, if it be not thy fault that the thing is not performed. 'Yea but it is a thing of that nature, as that thy life is not worth the while, except it may be performed.' If it be so, upon condition that thou be kindly and lovingly disposed towards all men, thou mayest be gone. For even then, as much as at any time, art thou in a very good estate of performance, when thou doest die in charity with those, that are an obstacle unto thy performance.

plain_english: Remember that your mind has a special nature. When it gathers itself together and looks inward, it becomes completely unconquerable. It needs nothing else but this: it cannot be forced. Even when it acts against reason itself, it still fights back. How much stronger it is when reason helps it judge things clearly? So make this your strongest defense: a mind free from overwhelming emotions. No one has a stronger or better protected refuge than this. Anyone who doesn't see this truth lacks wisdom. Anyone who sees it but doesn't use this refuge is foolish.
original_excerpt: Remember that thy mind is of that nature as that it becometh altogether unconquerable, when once recollected in herself, she seeks no other content than this, that she cannot be forced: yea though it so fall out, that it be even against reason itself, that it cloth bandy. How much less when by the help of reason she is able to judge of things with discretion? And therefore let thy chief fort and place of defence be, a mind free from passions. A stronger place, (whereunto to make his refuge, and so to become impregnable) and better fortified than this, hath no man. He that seeth not this is unlearned. He that seeth it, and betaketh not himself to this place of refuge, is unhappy.

plain_english: Stick to the bare facts of what happens to you. Don't add your own spin. Someone tells you that so-and-so spoke badly of you. Fine — that's what happened. But you weren't actually hurt by it. That's just your opinion talking, and you need to cut that out. I see that my child is sick. Yes, he's sick — I can see that. But I can't see that his life is in danger. That's me adding my own fears. This is how you must think. Stick to what you can actually observe. Don't pile on your own worries and opinions. Or if you do add something, make sure you understand how the world really works.
original_excerpt: Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in the world.

plain_english: Is the cucumber bitter? Throw it away. Are there thorns in the path? Go around them. That's enough. Don't start asking yourself, "What's the point of these things in the world?" Anyone who understands how nature works will laugh at you for that. It's like going into a carpenter's shop or a shoemaker's shop and complaining about the wood shavings and scraps left over from their work.
original_excerpt: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them. Let this suffice. Add not presently speaking unto thyself, What serve these things for in the world? For, this, one that is acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it; as a carpenter would or a shoemaker, if meeting in either of their shops with some shavings, or small remnants of their work, thou shouldest blame them for it.

plain_english: When merchants have goods they can't sell, they keep them in their shops for a while because they have nowhere else to put them. But the universe has no such storage problem. Here's what makes nature's skill so amazing: she sets her own boundaries, and whatever seems corrupted, old, or useless within those limits, she transforms back into herself. She makes new things from these old materials. She doesn't need to look outside herself for fresh supplies or for some dump where she can throw away what's completely rotten. She is completely self-sufficient in space, materials, and creativity.
original_excerpt: And yet those men, it is not for want of a place where to throw them that they keep them in their shops for a while: but the nature of the universe hath no such out-place; but herein doth consist the wonder of her art and skill, that she having once circumscribed herself within some certain bounds and limits, whatsoever is within her that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it into herself, and of these very things can make new things; so that she needeth not to seek elsewhere out of herself either for a new supply of matter and substance, or for a place where to throw out whatsoever is irrecoverably putrid and corrupt. Thus she, as for place, so for matter and art, is herself sufficient unto herself.

plain_english: Don't be lazy or careless in what you do. Don't be loose and wild in your actions. Don't be argumentative and difficult when you talk with others. Don't let your mind wander and chase after fantasies. Don't shrink your soul down small. Don't let it burst out wildly or launch into fury. And never be without something worthwhile to do.
original_excerpt: Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations. Not basely to contract thy soul; nor boisterously to sally out with it, or furiously to launch out as it were, nor ever to want employment.

plain_english: 'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they attack me with curses.' So what? Can't your mind stay pure, wise, calm, and just through all of this? Think of a spring of sweet, clear water. Someone standing nearby curses it, but the water keeps flowing just as sweet and clear. Even if dirt or dung gets thrown in, it's scattered right away and the water runs clear again. It can't be stained or poisoned. So what must I do to have a flowing spring inside myself, not just a stagnant well? Work constantly toward real freedom with kindness, and toward true simplicity and humility.
original_excerpt: 'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they persecute my person with curses.' What then? May not thy mind for all this continue pure, prudent, temperate, just? As a fountain of sweet and clear water, though she be cursed by some stander by, yet do her springs nevertheless still run as sweet and clear as before; yea though either dirt or dung be thrown in, yet is it no sooner thrown, than dispersed, and she cleared. She cannot be dyed or infected by it. What then must I do, that I may have within myself an overflowing fountain, and not a well? Beget thyself by continual pains and endeavours to true liberty with charity, and true simplicity and modesty.

plain_english: If you don't know what the world is, you don't know where you are. If you don't know what the world was made for, you can't know its qualities or nature. Anyone who lacks either of these things also doesn't know what he was made for. So what do you think of someone who cares deeply about the noise and applause of people who don't know where they are or what they are? Do you want praise from someone who curses himself three times in an hour? Do you want to please someone who doesn't please himself? Or do you think he pleases himself when he regrets almost everything he does?
original_excerpt: He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world. Now he that in either of these is to seek, for what he himself was made is ignorant also. What then dost thou think of that man, who proposeth unto himself, as a matter of great moment, the noise and applause of men, who both where they are, and what they are themselves, are altogether ignorant? Dost thou desire to be commended of that man, who thrice in one hour perchance, doth himself curse himself? Dost thou desire to please him, who pleaseth not himself? or dost thou think that he pleaseth himself, who doth use to repent himself almost of everything that he doth?

plain_english: Not only should we share breath with the air around us, but we should also share mind with the rational force that surrounds all things. That force spreads everywhere by its own nature, if we know how to draw it in. It passes through everything, just like air does, if we can breathe it in.
original_excerpt: Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that rational substance, which compasseth all things. For, that also is of itself, and of its own nature (if a man can but draw it in as he should) everywhere diffused; and passeth through all things, no less than the air doth, if a man can but suck it in.

plain_english: Wickedness in general does not hurt the world. One person's wickedness does not hurt others. It only hurts the person who does wrong. And he has been given a gift — whenever he truly wants to change, he can free himself from it right away. My neighbor's choices are not my concern, just like his life or his body are not my concern. We were made to help each other, but our minds still belong to ourselves alone. Otherwise, another person's wickedness could become my problem. God would not allow that. He would not let another person have the power to make me unhappy. Nothing can do that except my own wickedness.
original_excerpt: Wickedness in general doth not hurt the world. Particular wickedness doth not hurt any other: only unto him it is hurtful, whosoever he be that offends, unto whom in great favour and mercy it is granted, that whensoever he himself shall but first desire it, he may be presently delivered of it. Unto my free-will my neighbour's free-will, whoever he be, (as his life, or his bode), is altogether indifferent. For though we are all made one for another, yet have our minds and understandings each of them their own proper and limited jurisdiction. For else another man's wickedness might be my evil which God would not have, that it might not be in another man's power to make me unhappy: which nothing now can do but mine own wickedness.

plain_english:
The sun seems to pour out everywhere. And it does spread out, but it doesn't spill out carelessly. Its spreading is more like stretching or extending. That's why sunbeams are called rays — from the word meaning "to stretch out."

You can see what a sunbeam is like when sunlight comes through a small hole into a dark room. It always travels in a straight line. When it hits something solid that air can't pass through, it gets blocked and stops. But it doesn't slide away or fall down. It just stays there.

That's how your mind should spread its influence — not spilling out everywhere, but extending deliberately. Whatever obstacles your mind meets, don't attack them violently or charge at them. Don't collapse either. Just stand firm and give light to whatever can receive it. If something can't receive your light, that's its own fault and loss. It's cutting itself off from what you offer.
original_excerpt: The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension. For therefore are the beams of it called ἀκτῖνες from the word ἐκτείνεσθαι to be stretched out and extended. Now what a sunbeam is, thou mayest know if thou observe the light of the sun, when through some narrow hole it pierceth into some room that is dark. For it is always in a direct line. And as by any solid body, that it meets with in the way that is not penetrable by air, it is divided and abrupted, and yet neither slides off, or falls down, but stayeth there nevertheless: such must the diffusion in the mind be; not an effusion, but an extension. What obstacles and impediments soever she meeteth within her way, she must not violently, and by way of an impetuous onset light upon them; neither must she fall down; but she must stand, and give light unto that which doth admit of it. For as for that which doth not, it is its own fault and loss, if it bereave itself of her light.

plain_english: Someone who fears death either fears having no awareness at all, or fears that their awareness will be different. But they should comfort themselves with this: either there will be no awareness and therefore no sense of suffering, or if there is awareness, then it means another life — and so no real death.
original_excerpt: He that feareth death, either feareth that he shall have no sense at all, or that his senses will not be the same. Whereas, he should rather comfort himself, that either no sense at all, and so no sense of evil; or if any sense, then another life, and so no death properly.

plain_english: All people are made for each other. So either teach them to do better, or put up with them.
original_excerpt: All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or bear with them.

plain_english: The mind doesn't move like an arrow. When the mind is careful and cautious, turning this way and that to examine things closely, it still reaches its target just as well as when it moves without such care.
original_excerpt: The motion of the mind is not as the motion of a dart. For the mind when it is wary and cautelous, and by way of diligent circumspection turneth herself many ways, may then as well be said to go straight on to the object, as when it useth no such circumspection.

plain_english: Look deeply into the mind of everyone you deal with. And let others see clearly into your own mind too.
original_excerpt: To pierce and penetrate into the estate of every one's understanding that thou hast to do with: as also to make the estate of thine own open, and penetrable to any other.
